paper_title: Mobile AI Factory: Building Specialized Language Models for Your Mobile Device

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Small language models (SLMs) running on mobile devices can keep user data private and work without connectivity. But they perform well only when fine-tuned for the target task and sized for the target device, a process that today requires repeated expert tuning. We present {\it Mobile AI Factory}, an agentic system that builds a fine-tuned, quantized SLM for a given task and phone. Given a task specification and a target phone, an orchestrator LLM chooses whether to tune hyperparameters, mine real data, or generate synthetic examples, while fixed rules roll back changes that hurt accuracy. The factory searches from small to large models across base models and quantizations, adapts its accuracy goal as it searches, and uses real measurements of the target phone across inference engines and backends. We evaluate Mobile AI Factory on ten tasks and four Android phones. On an unseen testset, its on-device models outperform two five-shot frontier models on five tasks, by up to 0.34, and match them on three more. Its search comes within 0.03 of exhaustively training all 27 model variants on an entity extraction task, while using 19$\times$ less GPU time. Phone measurements also matter: the best configuration changes across phones. Without phone measurements, Claude Opus 5.5, given the full hardware and model specifications, misses the app's requirements in 25\% of easy and moderate cases and in 60\% of hard ones. Code is available at: https://github.com/evanly-gh/SLM_Factory.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Small language models that run directly on mobile devices
could enable numerous applications. For example, a key-
board app could rewrite a hastily typed message into a more
professional response, an email client could summarize mes-
sages and draft replies, and a voice assistant could help users
with motor impairments fill out forms and navigate appli-
cations. Running these models on the device, rather than in
the cloud, has two key advantages. First, sensitive data, like
a patient’s medication schedule or a customer’s bank details,
can remain on the device. Second, applications can operate in
scenarios where connectivity is limited or intermittent, such
as translating a conversation on a hiking trail or providing
navigation when a vehicle loses network access.
sections.content: Figure 1: Mobile AI Factory. It takes task specification and budget, and builds specialized model for phone. Smartphones now include capable CPUs and GPUs, and mobile inference engines such as llama.cpp and MNN can run quantized SLMs at practical speeds [12]. The harder problem is building the models themselves. Each application needs model that is trained for its task and small enough to run on the target phone. Even with training data available, developers still need to fine-tune base model, iterate on accuracy, decide on the model size and quantization level, and test the resulting model on the target phone. This process must be manually repeated by human expert for every phone model, which makes it impractical for all but the largest companies. The Facebook app alone runs on more than ten thousand smartphone and tablet models spanning many distinct SoCs [56]. New phones are released every year, and roughly two new open foundation models are released every week [38]. configuration that performs well on one phone may perform poorly, or fail entirely, on another. For example, in our measurements, llama.cpp GPU prefill is 5.4 faster than CPU prefill on the OnePlus 15, but 7.4 slower on the OnePlus 8 Pro. Similarly, Qwen3-4B at 8-bit precision decodes 12.613.8 tokens/s on the OnePlus 15, but only 0.74.8 tokens/s on the OnePlus 8 Pro. We ask the following question: given task specification and target phone, can we automatically produce finetuned, quantized SLM that meets both the tasks accuracy Mobile AI Factory, October, 2026 Evan Li, Krishna Deshpande, Wen Cheng and Shyamnath Gollakota goal and the phones resource budget? The developer inputs the specification, which includes any available data sources, the evaluation metric, verifier for the models outputs, optionally an accuracy goal, and the apps resource requirements, such as prefill and decode speed, memory, and energy. This is difficult because we cannot know in advance which model will meet these requirements while achieving the best accuracy. Further, we may not know how large model task needs until we train it. We present Mobile AI Factory, an agentic system that builds specialized SLMs. Its core is loop that curates training data, fine-tunes and evaluates model, then decides what to try next. An orchestrator LLM chooses one intervention per iteration, while fixed rules handle rollback, budgets, and model scaling. Three components support this loop: teacher model that generates synthetic data, held-out-data agent that prepares held-out set before training and shares only aggregate results with the orchestrator, and phone profiler that benchmarks models across quantization levels, runtimes, and backends once per phone, reusing the results across tasks to identify configurations that meet app requirements. At its core, our factory uses three key techniques. Agentic search with rollback and adaptive accuracy goals. We model each training attempt as pipeline of dataset, hyperparameters, and learning strategy. At each iteration, the orchestrator chooses one intervention: tuning hyperparameters (LoRA rank, scaling, learning rate, weight decay, and number of epochs), mining more real data (if available) from the tasks sources, or having the teacher generate synthetic examples aimed at the failure categories that hurt accuracy most. contamination check removes any row that also appears in the held-out test set. Since most interventions do not help, any change that lowers accuracy is rolled back to the best model so far, and the orchestrator tries something different. Finally, fixed accuracy target may be too easy for some tasks and unreachable for others. Instead we set the goal to the teacher models five-shot score on the task (zero-shot where five examples do not fit its context), with floor of 0.8. If the factory reaches the goal quickly or with little effort on the current model, the orchestrator can choose to raise it and continue its search. This lets it keep improving on tasks where the goal was set too low. Bucketed search from small to large models. models size depends on both its parameter count and its quantization: 2B model at 4 bits is smaller than 16-bit 0.8B model. We group all combinations of base model and quantization into 𝑁 buckets by size, and start with the smallest bucket. Within bucket, the orchestrator picks which combination to train. If accuracy stops improving before reaching the goal, the factory moves to the next bucket. This avoids two extremes: letting the orchestrator pick one combination from the whole pool, which gives no guarantee of small model, and training every combination, which is too expensive. Profiling the target phone. Whether model meets the apps requirements cannot be reliably determined from its specifications; it must be measured on the phone. The phone profiler measures prefill and decode speed, peak memory, and energy on the target phone for all combinations of base model, quantization, runtime (llama.cpp or MNN), and backend (CPU or GPU). Each phone is profiled once, and the profile is reused across all tasks. The profile also determines how to run the final model, since the best runtime and backend differ across phones, models, and quantization levels. The factory can then search only over models that meet the apps requirements on that phone, and the model it outputs is far more likely to run within them. We implement Mobile AI Factory using Claude Sonnet 5 as the orchestrator. Each run uses two NVIDIA L40S GPUs: one trains and scores the model, and the other hosts local teacher model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) that generates synthetic data. The model pool contains nine base models from 135M to 4B parameters, from the SmolLM2, Gemma 3, Qwen3, and Qwen3.5 families, each at 4-bit, 8-bit, and 16-bit precision, for 27 combinations. We group these into five buckets by size on disk, with boundaries at 300 MB, 750 MB, 1.5 GB, and 2.5 GB. We profile four Android phones, ranging from current flagship to budget phone whose GPU the inference engines cannot use due to the lack of OpenCL: the OnePlus 15, Galaxy S23, OnePlus 8 Pro, and Redmi 9A. We evaluate the factory on ten tasks: biomedical entity extraction, fine-grained entity extraction, calendar event extraction, function calling, command parsing, 151-way intent classification, spam detection, emotion detection, grammatical error correction, and dialogue summarization. Our results are as follows: On an unseen test set, the factorys small models outperform both Claude Sonnet 5 and DeepSeek v4 Flash, given five examples, on five tasks, by 0.024 to 0.342, and match them on three more. The gains are largest where the output format is strict: on biomedical entity extraction, 517 MB model scores 0.828, while Claude scores 0.652 with five examples. With the phone in the loop, the factory returns models whose profiled cost on the phone meets every limit. On Galaxy S23 whose limits rule out the factorys best model for call summaries, it returns model within 0.013 of it. Phone measurements cannot be replaced by reasoning. Given every specification but no real measurements, Claude Opus 5.5, with high reasoning effort enabled, misses the apps requirements in quarter of easy and moderate cases, and in 60% of hard ones. It misjudges run-time memory and the backend, neither of which appears on spec sheet. Mobile AI Factory: Building Specialized Language Models for Your Mobile Device Mobile AI Factory, October, 2026 After the first fine-tune, search adds median of 8 points on the smallest models and 2 points on the largest. On biomedical entity extraction, bucketed search comes within 3 points of training all 27 combinations at nineteenth of the GPU time. When goal is reached within few iterations, the orchestrator raises it; in seven of the nine runs where raise led to more training, the model improved, by 3.6 points. Contributions. (1) We present Mobile AI Factory, to our knowledge the first agentic system that builds fine-tuned, quantized SLM for given task and given phone. In contrast to optimizing accuracy on single model [3], our factory searches from small to large models and uses measurements from the target phone. (2) We profile four Android phones across 364 configurations (104 per phone with GPU, 52 on the Redmi 9A) of model, quantization, runtime, and backend, and show that the best configuration differs across phones, models, and quantization levels. (3) We evaluate the factory on ten tasks and show that, on unseen test sets, its on-device models outperform two five-shot frontier models on five tasks and match them on three more, and that, with the phone in the loop, it returns models whose profiled cost on the phone meets every limit.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Agentic and Automated Fine-Tuning. Classical AutoML automates model selection and hyperparameter search over predefined spaces [6, 14, 16, 30, 35, 49], but cannot change the training data. MLE-bench [11] and Kaggle-style agents [25, 43] evaluate agents on end-to-end modeling tasks. AutoMLAgent [50] proposes multiple LLM agents to go from task description to working model, but not one optimized to particular device. Prompt optimizers [2, 28, 60] instead improve the prompts given to fixed model. Over the past year, researchers have begun using agents to fine-tune language models [31]. PostTrainBench [45] studies whether agents can post-train base language models under fixed compute budget. Pioneer Agent [3], the closest work, acquires data, builds evaluation sets, and trains small language models by jointly searching over data, hyperparameters, and learning strategy. Other work uses agents to curate or process training data for fixed student model [23, 37], or to generate synthetic data aimed at the students weaknesses [62]. Tools such as Slemify [4] automate fixed pipeline of synthetic data generation, fine-tuning, and quantization for models served on CPU servers. These systems share key assumption: the model they produce will run on server, so accuracy is the only objective. On phone, this assumption breaks in four ways. First, search that maximizes accuracy favors the largest model. Our factory instead treats the base model and its quantization level as single choice and searches from small to large, moving to larger model only when the current one stops improving. Second, model evaluated at full precision may not be able to run on the phone; 4-bit quantization can significantly lower the accuracy: on the same weights, MNNs default 4-bit export loses up to 0.19 (3). Our factory therefore scores every model after quantization. Third, the same model can meet the apps requirements on one phone and fail them on another, since the best runtime and backend differ across phones, and even frontier model given full specifications picks configuration that fails the apps limits in 60% of hard cases (5.3). Our factory uses measured profile of the target phone to decide which models to search and how the final model runs. Finally, tasks differ widely in difficulty, so fixed accuracy target is either unreachable or trivial. Our factory sets its goal from teacher model and raises it when the goal is met easily. Hardware-Aware Model Design. Hardware-aware neural architecture search includes device cost in the search objective, either by measuring latency on real phones [48] or by estimating it with predictors and lookup tables [10, 55]. Other work specializes networks for different devices [9] or for microcontrollers [33]. nn-Meter [63] predicts DNN inference latency, and [20, 51] search quantization and compression policies with hardware feedback. These methods design architectures or compression policies for given dataset, rather than adapting pretrained language models to new task. In contrast, we fine-tune pretrained language models for new task and treat quantization as part of the search. We also measure each configuration on the phone instead of predicting it, since run-time memory and the best backend differ in ways predictor or specification sheet may miss. Recent work also gives LLM agents feedback from hardware, to write embedded firmware [32, 46, 58, 61, 64] or generate inference engines [26]. These systems optimize the software around model, or preserve model that already performs the task. Our factory instead builds the task capability itself, for language models on phones. Adapting Models to Devices. NestDNN [15] builds multicapacity models that trade accuracy for resources at runtime, LegoDNN [19] scales models block by block to fit each device, and AdaptiveNet [54] adapts deployed model to diverse edge environments. These systems start from model that already performs the task and adjust its size. Our factory starts from task specification, builds the task capability through fine-tuning and data, and chooses the model, its precision, and its runtime from measurements of each phone. On-Device LLM Inference and Measurement. number of engines run quantized language models on phones, including llama.cpp [12], MNN [24, 53], MLC-LLM [40], and ExecuTorch [39]. Research systems further reduce latency using mobile NPUs [57] and activation sparsity [59], and Mobile AI Factory, October, 2026 Evan Li, Krishna Deshpande, Wen Cheng and Shyamnath Gollakota MobileLLM [36] designs sub-billion-parameter models for phones. Prior work also measures LLM performance, memory, and energy across phones and frameworks [29, 42], profiles models on real devices in device farms [44], and selects backend for each device at runtime [7, 39]. These systems run or measure an existing model. In contrast, our factory builds the model, and uses per-phone measurements to decide how it runs on each target phone. Training Data and Quantization. Prior work shows that data generated by teacher model lets small models perform well beyond their size [1, 41, 52], and that small set of highquality examples can outperform larger one [66]. Small models can outperform much larger models [21, 65]; our factory automates this process and targets it at phone. Later work targets this data at the students failures [27, 62], filters it for quality [5], and warns that self-generated data can narrow models outputs [47]. Our factory uses synthesis as an intervention, anchored to real training examples and filtered by programmatic checks before training. Similarly, models are typically fine-tuned with LoRA [22] and quantized after training [13, 17, 34]. In contrast, our factory makes quantization part of the search, choosing between larger model at lower precision and smaller one at higher precision, and scores both after quantization. Unlike systems that fine-tune on the phone [18], our factory runs on server.

Deploying a small language model on a phone requires choos-

quantization. These choices depend heavily on the phone.

We benchmark 26 of the 27 model variants that Mobile AI Factory searches over: nine base models from 135M to 4B parameters, each at 4, 8 and 16 bits, except the 16-bit Qwen3.5-4B, which exceeds the RAM of two of our four phones. sections.title:
4.1 Agentic Architecture Overview
Fig. 4 shows our two-stage system. The setup stage, run
once per task, looks up the target phone’s measured profile,
removes every configuration that exceeds the developer’s
budgets on that phone, and picks the inference engine and
backend for each remaining variant. The search loop runs
until the goal is met or the budget runs out.
sections.content: The orchestrator LLM decides which intervention to try next, which model to try within tier, and whether to raise the accuracy goal. It does not decide when to stop, when to roll back, or when to move to larger model; those are deterministic rules. We split the roles this way for two reasons. First, run calls the orchestrator most often when it is stuck, so the rule that notices it is stuck should not depend on the orchestrator. Second, most of the orchestrators ideas do not work: in the run with the most iterations (nested intent parsing, 109 evaluations, 104 of them interventions), 88% of the interventions made the model worse and were rolled back. The rules ensure steady progress. Each run uses three models: the orchestrator, local teacher that writes synthetic training data, and the small model being built for the phone.

sections.title:
4.2.1 Phone Profiles and Feasibility. We measure each phone
once, using the protocol in §3. A configuration is one of
the model variants run on one engine (llama.cpp or MNN)
and one backend (CPU or GPU). For each configuration, the
profile stores prefill and decode throughput, peak memory,
and energy per token; configurations that crash, run out of
memory, or are rejected by the GPU driver are stored as
failures.
sections.content: The developer gives budgets for typical request: latency, memory and energy. The factory computes each configurations latency from its measured throughput and the requests prompt and output lengths, and drops configurations that exceed budget or failed on this phone. For each surviving variant, it keeps the engine and backend that decode fastest on that phone. The factory groups the feasible variants into five tiers by their size on disk, with boundaries at 300 MB, 750 MB, 1.5 GB and 2.5 GB. 2B model at 4 bits (1.3 GB) thus shares the third tier with 0.6B model at 16 bits (1.4 GB). Of the 27 variants, 6, 5, 5, 4 and 7 fall in tiers 1 to 5. phone profile only removes variants; it does not change the tier boundaries.

sections.title:
4.3 Search Loop
The loop decides which model to train (§4.3.1), what to
change (§4.3.2) and whether a change helped (§4.3.3).
sections.content: Small-to-Large Search. The factory starts in the cheap4.3.1 est tier and moves up only when that tier stops improving. Escalation rule. The factory escalates when the score has not risen by more than 0.02 over the last 15 evaluations, or after 30 evaluations in one tier without reaching the goal. Both counts include rolled-back attempts. On escalation, the Mobile AI Factory: Building Specialized Language Models for Your Mobile Device Mobile AI Factory, October, 2026 Figure 4: Mobile AI Factory. setup stage reads the phones measured profile and builds frozen evaluation set; loop then curates data, trains, scores the quantized artifact and decides what to do next. Dark orange is the orchestrator LLM, and light orange nodes call it. Blue nodes, including rollback and the decision to escalate, are deterministic code. orchestrator picks one variant in the next tier. The run keeps its training data, and the rest of the search starts over. Increasing the goal. When the run reaches its goal, the factory stores the result and asks the orchestrator whether to raise the goal, by at least 0.005 above the highest goal so far and to at most 0.99. raised goal sends the run back into the loop. The orchestrator may lower the goal when failures look like model size limit, but only after raise, and never below the starting goal. Output. The run returns the best model in each tier it visited, with its engine and backend. Since the search climbs from the cheapest tier, the developer reads off the cheapest one that meets their bar. If no tier does, the run returns its best model and why it stopped: tiers, steps or time ran out.

sections.title:
4.3.2 The Orchestrator and Its Interventions. In each itera-
tion, the orchestrator proposes exactly one change.
sections.content: Input and output. The orchestrator sees the evaluators report (the overall score, accuracy on easy, medium and hard rows, and the most common failure categories from the tasks own scorer, such as wrong entity boundaries or call to an undeclared function), and the run memory, built from the search graph, which lists every attempt, whether it was kept, and what has failed since the last improvement. It returns JSON object, naming the change, its parameters and hypothesis. The factory validates it, and replaces hyperparameter setting already tried on the same data with an untried neighbor. Hyperparameters. hyperparameter intervention holds the data fixed and adjusts up to five values: LoRA rank, the ratio of 𝛼 to rank, weight decay, learning rate and epochs. Batch shape follows from the GPU and dropout is fixed at zero. Data. data change adds rows and keeps the best hyperparameters so far. Rows come from two sources. Mining first reads further into the tasks own sources, and searches the web for new datasets only when those are exhausted, giving up after two empty rounds. Targeted synthesis has the teacher write 25600 rows per failure category, in proportion to its failure count, and drops category whose count does not fall. Synthesis passes three gates. (1) The teacher must score at least 0.80 on the task with five real examples, the way synthesis prompts it, or synthesis is off for the run; our main runs bypass this gate on seven tasks (5.1). Examples matter: on biomedical entity extraction the teacher scores 0.13 without them and 0.32 with five. (2) Each row passes programmatic check where one exists, for example that every extracted entity appears verbatim in its text. (3) The teacher can check each row against the brief (4.2.2), using only real examples as references; our runs turn this check off where strict programmatic check exists and, on the other tasks, record its verdicts without dropping rows. The training set only grows; rows leave only through quality control, the firewall, or the rollback of the change that added them. Rollbacks. Three mechanisms limit each failure to one iteration. Training always restarts from the base model, so rollback exactly restores the previous behavior. Control then returns to the orchestrator, which must try different change rather than repeat the same regression. watchdog stops Mobile AI Factory, October, Evan Li, Krishna Deshpande, Wen Cheng and Shyamnath Gollakota runs that stop making progress, like three consecutive synthesis rounds that add nothing or training set that shrinks by 25% (or 1,000 rows) in one step. We require repeated or large failures so the watchdog does not trigger on noise; we added it after one run spent eight hours on eight data changes that added no examples. Scoring Each Iteration. The setup stage freezes held4.3.3 out evaluation set that training cannot access (4.2.3). The loop adds three rules. Each iteration merges the adapter, exports 4and 8-bit models to their deployment format, loads them in the target engine, and scores them on the held-out set; 16-bit models are scored in Transformers. For MNN, we use 4-bit HQQ with 32-weight blocks because its default quantization loses up to 0.19 accuracy (3). The evaluator returns scores, failure counts, and the fraction of parseable outputs, but not the evaluation rows. This separates wrong answers from malformed outputs. Any decision that quotes held-out row is rejected. The base model is the first candidate, and any fine-tuned model that scores worse is discarded, so the loop can conclude that fine-tuning does not help. failed evaluation is recorded as missing, not zero. An early run used zero and incorrectly credited fine-tuning with gain of 0.85.

Mining carries 48% of the gain on the smallest tier, synthesis 77% on the third, and hyperparameters 82% on the largest (Fig. 6b). This does not mean small models need data and large ones need tuning. First, mining runs out early, so later tiers fall back on the other two. Second, training data carried to larger model improves its first fine-tune, which falls outside the search. Third, gain goes to whichever step happened to be kept, so different order could split the same total differently. On seven tasks the teacher scored below 0.80, which by default turns synthesis off (4.3.2). We allowed synthesis on those runs anyway. It tests whether the teacher can do the task, but the teachers job is to write training rows. On nested parsing, the teacher scores 0.02 with five examples, yet 90% of the rows it writes pass the tasks check, and synthesis carried 60% of that tasks search gain. Writing correct example is easier than solving new one, so better gate would test the teacher as writer.

sections.title:
6 Discussion and Limitations
A developer still provides the task specification: data sources,
the metric, and a verifier for model outputs. Our results sug-
gest that the verifier matters most. Rejecting malformed out-
puts made synthetic data usable, while tasks where few gen-
erated rows survived quality control saw little benefit from
synthesis. Building this harness is the most hand-engineered
part of the pipeline. An agent that decomposes a task into
its type, such as classification, extraction or generation, and
assembles a matching scorer and verifier would make the
factory far more autonomous. So would an early check of
synthetic-data survival rates.
sections.content: We also restrict the factory to predefined set of decoder models from 135M to 4B. This is practical when developers prefer specific model vendors, but the restriction is not fundamental. The factory could instead download candidate base models on demand, and once task is known to be classification, add encoder models of 150M parameters, far smaller than any model in our pool. Training is LoRA finetuning only; preference optimization, reinforcement learning or distillation from larger model are natural additions. Synthesis writes few hundred rows per round from local 35B teacher. This keeps each round cheap and targeted, but may cap what synthesis can add; larger rounds from stronger teacher are worth exploring. Our phone profiles cover CPUs and GPUs. Recent work shows that mobile NPUs can process prompts an order of magnitude faster while offering little decode advantage over CPUs [8]. Adding NPUs would require only extending the hardware profile, and would make backend selection even more important. We also measure each configuration alone, from cool start, at one prompt length, with four threads, and with the phone otherwise idle. deployed model shares the phone with other apps, other models and changing thermal state, so sustained and concurrent use, and longer prompts, may change which configurations meet requirement. Profiling phone is slow, largely because it must cool between runs, but this cost is paid once and shared across tasks. Future work could measure only subset of configurations on new phone and predict the rest, while validating those predictions before the factory relies on them.

sections.title:
7 Conclusion
We present Mobile AI Factory, an agentic system that builds
a fine-tuned, quantized small language model for a given
task and phone. We showed that the right model and configu-
ration change from phone to phone, and that even a frontier
model cannot make this choice without measurements.
sections.content: Taking step back, ML and agent researchers mainly optimize metrics and rarely think about mobile devices. Mobile systems researchers, on the other hand, build inference engines and take the model as given. Mobile AI Factory suggests near-future in which agents build many phone-specific small, specialized models, and rebuild them as new phones and open base models are released. The same approach could extend beyond phones to wearables and embedded devices. We evaluated the models on unseen test sets that the factory never used for training or model selection: the finetuned model, its untrained base, and both frontier models given the same five examples as in Table 3  (Table 5)  . Spam detections held-out set took the whole test split, leaving only five unused spam messages, so we could not check it on unseen rows. The fine-tuned model beats its untrained base on every task, by 0.13 to 0.83, except function calling, where the untrained 4B model is already strong and fine-tuning adds 0.008. Most fine-tuned scores are lower than on the held-out set. On nested parsing, entity extraction and function calling, they drop by 0.0350.037 while the untrained model barely moves. On intent classification and grammar correction, the untrained model drops just as much, so the unseen test set data are simply harder. Against frontier models given five examples, the factorys model wins five tasks on the unseen test set, by 0.024 to 0.342: biomedical extraction, calendar extraction, nested parsing, entity extraction and dialogue summarization. Three tasks Figure 10: Best score per tier, starting from (a) 100 and (b) 151 real rows, with and without synthesis, against full real data. The x-axis gives each tiers model. are ties, within the noise floor: emotion classification, grammar correction, and intent classification with the goal at 0.99. Two are losses: function calling, and intent classification with the default goal, which stops on 360M model. Compared with the held-out set, grammar correction moves from win to tie, and intent classification at goal 0.99 moves from tie in our favor to one against. Synthetic Data under Data Scarcity With thousands of real rows, synthetic rows made up only 3 22% of each training set. So, we starved two tasks of real data: 100 rows for spam detection, and 151 for intent classification, one per intent. Each task ran twice from the same rows, with mining off and the goal set to 0.99, with and without synthesis data. Synthesis won all ten tier comparisons  (Fig. 10)  , eight of them by more than our 0.015 noise level and four of them by more than 0.03. Tiers within run share growing training set, so they are not independent. How much synthesis helped depended on what limited the small model. On spam detection, the 360M model scores 0.637 from 100 real rows and 0.935 with 362 generated rows added, close to its 0.944 on 4,045 mostly real rows. Without synthesis, only the 0.8B to 4B models reached that level. For the intent task, an example for each of 151 intents is too few for any model. Synthesis added 0.0130.059 at every tier and ended at 0.910, within 0.027 of the full-data run. Without it, no model passed 0.889. We reran every task with only 100 real rows (151 for intent classification, one per intent), mining off and synthesis enabled. Nested parsing kept its full-data score, but its loader always adds fixed 674-row in-domain adaptation set, so we leave it out of the counts that follow. Four of the other nine tasks retained at least 97% of their full-data score. Calendar extraction kept 98%, but only on the 4B model; the 0.8B model fell 0.18 behind, suggesting real data matters more for smaller models. Grammar correction and summarization lost Mobile AI Factory: Building Specialized Language Models for Your Mobile Device Mobile AI Factory, October, 2026 710%, while entity and emotion tasks lost 1630%. Teacher accuracy did not predict this loss. The two largest drops came on the two tasks where the fewest synthetic rows passed quality control: 3% for biomedical extraction and 24% for fine-grained entities, against more than 60% on every other task. Emotion classification points to second limit: 99% of its rows passed, but with 28 labels and 100 rows it starts with under four examples per label, and it lost 16%. This pass rate is cheap to estimate before relying on synthesis. Hardware requirements Tables 79 list the 60 requirements used in 5.3. Each deploys one of our ten tasks in way an app would use it, on one phone. requirement sets four limits: peak memory, minimum prefill speed, minimum decode speed, and maximum energy per request. configuration meets the requirement only if it meets all four. The kind of deployment sets the memory budget and the response time  (Table 6)  . fixed memory budget is capped at 25% of the phones RAM, which matters only on the 4 GB Redmi 9A. The tasks real request then sets the speeds: prefill must process the requests input within the first-token time, and decode must finish the answer within the remaining time. The fixed part of each prompt, such as instructions, label lists and tool schemas, is computed once and cached, so request prefills only its input. summary the user reads as it streams instead needs at least 5 tokens/s. The energy budget is share of the phones battery divided by the deployments requests per day. The same deployment therefore has different limits on different phones. The tier of requirement is the share of the phones configurations that meet it: easy if at least 60% do, moderate if 3060% do, and hard if fewer than 30% do. From the 38 deployments run on all four phones, we chose 20 requirements per tier, spread across tasks, phones and deployments, and kept only requirements that at least one configuration meets.
